title: Roots of Unity
body:
The $n$ solutions of $z^n = 1$. By [[Complex Exponential]] they are

$$
\omega_k = e^{2\pi i k/n}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1
$$

which are $n$ points spaced evenly around the unit circle, starting at 1. De Moivre's theorem in
[[Polar Form]] (MATH 1203) is where they come from: raising to the $n$th power multiplies the angle
by $n$, so the angles that reach a multiple of $2\pi$ are the multiples of $2\pi/n$.

Two properties do all the work:

- **They are closed under multiplication**: $\omega_j \omega_k = \omega_{(j+k) \bmod n}$. Angles add
  and wrap. So the $n$th roots of unity form a [[Cyclic Group]] of order $n$ under multiplication,
  generated by $\omega_1$. This is the standard first example in [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]], and it is one
  of the few places where a group-theory fact is visibly load-bearing elsewhere in the degree.
- **They sum to zero** for $n > 1$, by symmetry or by the geometric series
  $\sum_k \omega^k = \frac{\omega^n - 1}{\omega - 1} = 0$. That cancellation *is* the discrete
  orthogonality relation, which is why the rows of the DFT matrix are orthogonal.

A root is **primitive** if its powers generate all $n$ of them, which is exactly when
$\gcd(k, n) = 1$. The [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] uses the primitive root
$\omega = e^{-2\pi i/n}$ and builds its matrix from $\omega^{kn}$, so the whole transform is powers
of one number.

The wrap-around is also what makes the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] possible: $\omega^2$ for size $N$
is the primitive root for size $N/2$, so the even-indexed subproblem is *the same transform, half
the size*. Divide and conquer falls out of the algebra rather than being imposed on it.
